blocks.x: What is your full name?
Sidney L. Dathvin Senior.
You have a son and a second name. That's right. When birth you were born?
Well, let's see, in 93, 65 years old.
You're 65? Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
You got a real voice up.
You played for him once.
I used to go to your house once, and you're doing the trombone. Yeah, yeah.
Oh yeah, tell about that story when you played the...
How did I play the trombone?

Well, I was playing the trombone. Well, how did I see the way that started? I couldn't find any trombone player or something. So it was easy to get a trumpet player. So I thought I'd go ahead and pick up on the trombone, see? And took a few lessons on the trombone. And I think one job, if I'm not mistaken, a job we played in Kenner. I think it was Kenner, Louisiana, someplace there. I hired Louis Armstrong to play. Louis Armstrong and Joe Lindsey. And I played the trombone. Louis played the cornet then, see? And I know it too, Louis. Yeah, and then I stayed playing the trombone for a while. And then, couldn't find no trumpet player. And I thought I'd go back on the trumpet again, you see? But this one time, I remember this board, talking about the board. Well, I think Manuel was playing on the board. Or they wanted to hire him. Who was that? You and...

No, they sent to me, coming from St. Louis. But on Easter Monday morning, you see? You know, when I gave him my award, they were going to organize a band. And sent for me to come and meet the both, coming in the office. Well, I gave them my award. And the time didn't come, he wrote, that is, the road last time. And so, uh... We, uh... We played with Oak, Dad. That's San Suo Hall. You remember that? Well... All right. I said, I showed Sidney the telegram on Monday night. You remember San Suo Hall? You forgot that? No, I remember.
We go down to the telephone exchange. And he was right there. Yeah, Holtz.

Get him to take me. And I agreed, I said, well, I'll answer a little bit. I said, if you're free to take trumpet players, it's a dance game. Well, they had a rope in the back. So, I don't know. I've seen that white thing before. And I didn't see it. So, they're great, Ted. So, uh... I went along when the time come. I had the band all made up. They had Bob Sharper. Was the leader of the band. I taught this out in Ed Allen up there. So, they had a... They had a lady I was playing the piano with. Until I... Go with him. Go with him. I'm getting a little bit of a question. So... When I agreed to go, unless they take Sydney.
You've been working, you say, at the Cotton Building, was that? Or something like that? They had a way in town. At a day job. Yeah.

So, what I did, while they go to the Wake, they get me there, Bob Sharper go. Bob Sharper turned the leadership over to Eddie Allen. And that made a hard feelings. That made a hard feeling. But when I go to St. Louis, Sidney didn't go to me, but... I go to St. Louis, when this guy, Captain, I want him to come to meet me at the train. At the train. At the train, the guy would say hello to me and all that, but he knew that I was the fella that he was looking for. You know, they had them big old-looking mind glasses. You know, I'll put... I'd like to know where the... Mel Pottson Building is at. Who are you? I told him, he said, Well, I come out here and wait for you. You're going to be the piano brother, yeah. So, the outbrain, he said, where to stop at. So, he carried me. Johnny Sensei and George Foster was living together. On that morning, Johnny Sensei had his son. His wife had a boy. He's now about... Boy must be now around about 39, ain't he?
39 years old.
Oh.
That's right. So, George?
This guy has a good memory, you know that?
Yeah, yeah.
George Foster and Johnny Sensei was living together in the house. We go back in the kitchen. This fella just that bit. See, they're right there. Oh.
When you were on the boat... Huh? Excuse me. When you were on the boat, you all had rooms in St. Louis too. You didn't live...
You didn't sleep on the boat. Well, no. I'll tell you. We didn't stay long enough. I was on the boat. You stayed...
You slept on the boat then? I told you. See?

Well, you... That's the first time. Yeah, you see. I got there in the morning... In the morning. In the morning. At night. We played. We played for a colored job. That's crazy. That was on a Monday night. Yeah.
Was that regular every Monday?
Every Monday, that happened. And the next guy was white.
Yeah.
Well, anyhow, this father leads me.
He wouldn't say nothing to me.

Wouldn't tell me all he do, right here he lives, and I knock on the door. It was George Foster's wife came in. So he goes back in the kitchen and talks and tells me what. I told him all these fellas, it's funny actually. He said, well I'll tell you. Be careful, he says. So... You made a mistake of one thing that you done while they don't like you. By taking DejVe with you and leaving Bob Schauffer going to organize the band. You see? They say, watch these guys who's not allowed to do your thing. He said, alright. We players. We leave, take a trip up to St. Paul. Down for our way. Yeah, the boat. Alright. Come down. Now, on the following Sunday, we had to meet him in Memphis. Remember? Yeah. You come on the boat, you had a brand new horn, a silver, you had a CG clone, a silver horn. You had to change it and get a gold horn because the band was Allie's gold band.
That's right. The gold band. I had to get a gold trumpet.
Yeah, yeah. You had to change your head. That's right. That's right. I met you about two o'clock in Memphis on a Sunday evening. And, uh, we had a little rehearsal.
We had a little rehearsal, man.
Yeah. And that night, we, uh, we played. And I went out to town.
You remember that place? Yeah, yeah.
I remember.

Yeah. So when they would pay off, I'd always get paid when I'd go on a boat. When they had an intermission to go get paid because I'd pay Callie up. Mr. Louise was on there, which is Vernon's wife now, but she was waking for me. And I'd always get my envelope there, and I'd go up there to Callie up. Well, old guy, he was watching, and he never saw me get my envelope, you know. And he had plenty of funny impressions about it. He noticed everything. You know, we always go play a chord when the boat was running down. We'd go and play after a hoist and go play a chord. Well, I didn't play chords. I'd go. Me and the cameraman was violent. And his wife used to sing. You know, he'd play like that. And the waiter would get ice cream, eat the ice cream, right? But they'd be playing chords. I had a guy who was a stool pigeon farmer. His name was Thomas, Walter Thomas, an outdoor player. And they had another one.
I remember him. Huh? Floyd Casey. Floyd Casey. That's right.
That's right. Look at his stool pigeon. He's stool pigeon.
You remember all those guys, too, don't you?
Some of them have another guy. I just believe you were talking about it. Yeah.
And they had another young fat boy. Cedric. Yeah, Eugene Cedric.
He was with Fats Waller. Fats Waller. That's the last time. Well, by the way, excuse me to interrupt one second. His father was a famous ragtime piano player, they say, around St. Louis.
Cedric's daddy? He was with Fats Waller. Fats Waller.
That's the last time. Well, by the way, excuse me to interrupt one second. His father was a famous ragtime piano player, they say, around St. Louis. Cedric's daddy?
Is that right?
His father, did you ever hear any of the ragtime piano players there that go out to Turpin's, that jazz land, or the Booker T. Washington Theater? Did you ever get around St. Louis?
No, not much, no. Did you hear that?
One other question while I interrupt you, Fats. Did most of the fellas have rooms then in St. Louis?
Well, coming down on the boat, we had our rooms.
I don't know. But most of them, would they live on the boat, or would they sleep in St. Louis? Yeah.
Well, they had permission to sleep on a boat too, and a boat was here, you see, but they'd go out in town and get a room. No, but he said St. Louis.
And St. Louis too, I wonder.

No, when you said, when I stayed in St. Louis, I think it was three or four summers that I went, I worked with Faith Marlborough's Band, when I had my room out in town. No one stayed on the boat in St. Louis, they operated out there.
No one stayed on the boat.

The only thing I ever stayed on the boat there was the deckhands, I imagine. That was all. But nobody lived on the boat. Only when you go up the river. That's right. When you're traveling down from St. Louis, you know, you're... That's right.

That's the only one for sure. That's right. Well, there's that one other dance too, that Vest, or somebody told me once where you started to play trombone, and the people that had hired the band, they didn't know what was going on when they saw you on trombone. They thought something's wrong here.
Well, they just thought I couldn't play the trombone, and they wanted me to play the trumpet, you see.

That's the blue rhythm club, we'll see. Blue rhythm club. Blue rhythm club. It's a big open place. All that in those trombone, so... Yeah, big guy in the dance field. Well, I know, but I don't see... It's my own band. It's my own band.

I understand that. They're playing for them people, but play this trumpet. The thing is, I had a trumpet player, I probably didn't play more trumpet than I could play, but still they wanted me to play the trumpet, you see what I mean?
You know you had that that night? You know you had? No, I don't.
I know all in Lillistat. You sure know. And you was playing the trombone?

What did? I know I'm a twi-a, and Louis Armstrong. So when they walk in, the fella said, he said, what do you say? Now you pull a little over my eyes, uh-uh, uh-uh, uh-uh. I don't know what I say. You remember he had to put a trombone down? And he take the horn up, and I know, this nigga out here fool with the music, you know? He was satisfied. Yeah, he was beatin' by it. He was satisfied. He was satisfied so long he saw us playin' the place, he started packin' up, you know? Well, he was satisfied he saw us stayin' there with that horn, that trumpet.

And Arnold was a fine trumpet player. He played all right here. Juarez, Tijuana, he played all around Mexico, you know? Because I remember when I first met Arnold Matoir, and he used to tell me about Tijuana and Juarez while we was playin' there. But he used to do very nice trumpet. Oh, he was? Yeah. Yeah. Nice trumpet play.
I never got to know him or hear him or know anything about him, very little except what some people have told me.
He played just like those Mexican guys, you know? Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah, and then when he got on the boats, then they put the old trombone down and went back on his trumpet. Then, uh, made a trip, then you come outta town, you organize your band, the Deadly Orchestra. Right? Yes, right. That's right. Used to be.

Can you ask once more about some of your arrangements with your big band? Did you all ever just do without the music altogether on any number and just play a whole head arrangement with a big ten or twelve piece band, or did you always have music?

Well, no, we didn't do that so much. We knew the arrangements as far as that's concerned. We knew them. Yeah, we knew them, you see? But we could sit there and play most of our, the whole program that night, you see? Because we remembered all the things by playing them, you see? Remember that.
Yeah, I was just wondering if they'd ever say, for instance, call it blues, like in B flat or something, and then they just play.
Oh, well that was just the blues, yeah, at times. Yeah, yeah, just the blues, yeah.
Yeah, and the whole band could improvise or maybe-
Well, we played an engagement in a place they call Bugaloosa in Louisiana.
The honky-tonk.

The honky-tonk. Okay. We got up there and start playing our big arrangements. Nobody want to dance. Nobody. They say, this band come from New York. This is the music they're playing. They come from New York. We don't want that kind of music. One fellow in the band said, let's play the blues. So when we played the blues, then they all got out and started hollering, and that's what they wanted, the blues. That's right. Yeah.
The other than the band did things like that too.
They didn't want that kind of music. Yeah, we played in- In- Muscatine, Iowa. Yeah.
Muscatine, Iowa.

I have 11 men in the band, and it's a big dance. And we had some guy by the name of Slim John or something. He played the accordion, that hillbilly stuff, you know. So we had an hour to play, and they would play an hour. So we started off playing our first hour. People were all crowded around the place, but nobody wouldn't dance. The kind of stuff we were putting out, they just didn't like that. So after our hour was up, and this band played, boy, the first number they hit, one of them old quadrille, little square dancers or something, and everybody got up and started dancing. So you know what I did the next day? I went to the music store and bought me a whole book of that kind of stuff that that band was putting on. We were rehearsing the whole day. And boy, when we started playing it, everybody danced in. We had them. We had them covered.

Speaking of trombone, I wonder if you could talk just for a minute or two about trombone players. Who was your favorite trombone player? You mentioned much George Field, but of all the different trombonists you've heard or worked with, who were some of the greatest that you remember? The best ones, or your favorites, you might say. Either people that worked with you or others that you heard when you were a kid?

I didn't know too many trombone players. I know the names of Vic Gasper and Buddy Johnson. You know Benirap? I never did know that guy, Benirap. I mean, he was a great trombone player, but I didn't know him.
You know Baptiste Benirap?
I didn't know that guy. I never knew he'd die.
I never knew he'd die. What about you?
Louis Nelson was the only one that Louis Nelson could play very good trombone when he didn't drink. Yeah, that's right.
When he didn't drink.

You know him. Yeah, I remember Dutre. He was a very good tromboneer. Roy Palmer? Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer. We started out together, yeah. Roy Palmer was also. Oh, yeah. And I knew Roy and Trombone. Roy was the one giving me lessons on the trombone. Roy Palmer. Roy Palmer was giving me lessons. I told him I don't like the trumpet. I said, I want to play the trombone. He said, alright. I used to go to Roy's house every day. So, but the thing was, I'd be playing the trombone, you see, and the next day I got to play a job playing cornet, and then it wouldn't work together then, you see. I couldn't blow both of those instruments.
How did Roy play in those days? Was he one of the best, I guess?
I think Roy was a pretty good trombone player. Pretty good. I think he was a very good trombone player.
Did he teach you with a regular method? That's right, that's right.

That's right. Good. Do you remember zoo robbers? And he sold me a horn, too. Oh, he did. He sold me a horn for a dollar and a half. Old horn he couldn't use. Every time I'd blow the thing, you know, bubbles would start coming out of it. Had a whole lot of soap, you know, on the end there, you know. When I start blowing, big bubbles. Blowing bubbles. Blowing bubbles, you know.
The slide would work, I guess, is a little bit. Did you know Zoo Robertson?

Very good. Zoo Robertson, he's one guy that wanted to take me with the 101 Ranch I remember. He told the man that I have a trumpet player for her. And the man sent two tickets. Well, I'm young and I told my mother about it. My mother wouldn't let me go. She wouldn't let me go. So, he had to send the tickets back. Is that sort of a Wild West show or like circuses?
That's right, along them kind of circuses.
That's what he's like, a small one, you know. Yeah. And you know Bebe Ridley. Oh, yeah.
Yeah, Bebe Ridley.

What did you remember? He played drums and trombone on them. Trombone, Celestine. Yeah, but he played drums, too, one time. That was Bebe Matthews. Bill Matthews, brother. Oh, yeah. Oh, Kid Ora, did you ever work with him? Oh, Kid Ora, I never did. I worked with him, you know, but I never was a member of the band. I worked with him. We'd work together, you know, and I'd play in the dance, where they'd have two bands. We'd catch each other on the corner, you know, advertising, and we'd play against each other, you know. Like Buck.
Yeah.
Were there any of the other real early bands that you remember hearing when you were a boy, aside from the Emmanuel Perez group? You mentioned the superior band with the…
The Olympia band, Freddie Keppert. That was Freddie Keppert's band. Yeah, the Olympia, the superior.
Remember who else was with Keppert when you'd hear him? I don't know those guys at all. I didn't know them.

I was quite young, you see. When you were watching the company. Yeah, that's right. I just listened, but I didn't know them. But if I'm not mistaken, one fellow played with him by the name of Piku, if I'm not mistaken. Did he? Played what? Piku played clarinet with that band. And AJ P. And AJ P. Rohn played violin, if I'm not mistaken. Freddie Keppert long years ago.
Yeah. Little San Diego. Yeah, Little San Diego.
Get there. I didn't know much about them then. Did you ever do any teaching?
Teach other trumpet players yourself? Of course a lot of people listen and maybe work with them bands too. But I mean, did you ever really give music lessons like Fess does? Well, at times, yeah.

At times, you know. But I didn't like it. You know. I didn't like it. I didn't like it. Did you travel much except for the boat? Did you ever go to New York or anything else? No, no, no. Well, we traveled, let's see, all parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida. That's the only places we traveled. On a bus or going to train? On a bus, on a bus, yeah. On a bus. What type of music did you enjoy? You worked with the big band more than you did with the small band, like the little
five or six piece band, or did you enjoy it? Well, I liked both of them. Both. After I started playing with the big band, you know, it was different than playing, you

know, with a small band, because with a small band everybody's out for itself, you know what I mean? Working all the time. Yeah. And in the big band, you don't play so much. You have your time when you got to play and time that you don't have to play. But with the, when we were having a six, five, six, seven piece band, well, you just played any time you felt like it. You had to be playing all the time.
You were the first big band that way, would you say, in New Orleans? Well, I would think I was.

I think I was, if I'm not mistaken. But you didn't think of Dixie. But I do know that we were the first one, the big band, to actually have really uniformed the band, all uniformed, you know. Yeah, that uniform. We had tuxed and then we had some blazes and, very good, looked very good. And after that, all the rest of the band began copping after us then. They all started doing the same thing, having uniforms. That was way back, boss. Way back. Hmm? I brought an issue. Just a minute. Sure, I thought it.
I'm a piano player here. This is your big band?
Yes, one of them in 1935 and 34,

70. That's the name of my band then. Yeah, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven. That's right, yeah. You remember most of those bands now? Let's see. The piano player here is Loving Good.
Oh, that's St. Louis. Yeah, that's Loving Good. And this is Porter. Porter's in San Diego. This is George Fleming.
He's out here in Berkeley. Wait a minute.
Poinnell here.
That's Poinnell. That's Poinnell saxophone player. And this is Riley, Judge Riley. He's the better drummer.
Judge Riley.

He's in Chicago. Yeah, it seems like I heard of him. This is a guy here. I picked him up in Mississippi somewhere. The trombone player by the name of Moran. And later years he played with, what, let's see. I think of the name of the And this is Eugene Ware. That's a trumpet player. That's the one that got stranded with one of those shows in New Orleans and I hired him to play in my band. He's in Indianapolis now. And this is Marcel. I got him out of Detroit. Singer. That's me in my picture. And this is New Orleans. Ransom, New Orleans. I got him out of Vicksburg, Mississippi. And this is Gishaw. Gishaw, he's in Chicago now. There was two brothers. Both of them played saxophone. One of those boys, one of them is in St. Louis. St. Louis, St. Louis. St. Louis, that's right. That's right.
Louis Nelson wasn't in that group.

No, no, no. That was a trombone player, Moran, right there. Yeah. Well, Louis Nelson used to get full, you know, and I'd high him and fire him and high him and fire him. He stopped drinking though. No, he did, huh? He was in good shape. Well, that's the way I carried my band all the time in different uniforms at that time. Oh, yeah, that's nice. Yeah. And the singer had on the dark. That's right.
That's right.
That's right. Yeah. Is that taken up on top of the boat?
That's right. That's right.
I don't want to top it. That's 23 years ago, eh? Hmm? Hmm?
That's 23 years ago, eh? No, I mean, 23.
Yeah, 23. Yeah, that's around, that's 33, 34, and 35. You mentioned the capital, I believe, and, uh? The steamer Sydney was the first boat.
Yeah. You ever play on the St. Paul?
On the St. Paul? On the St. Paul. I played on the St. Paul. 23.
Yeah, that's around, that's 33, 34, 35, this one here.
Now, which person, which other boats you played? You mentioned the Capitol, I believe, and the...
The Steamer Sydney was the first boat.
Yeah. You ever play on the St. Paul?
On the St. Paul. I played on the St. Paul. There was another boat. At night. Played on the Capitol. What about the JS? Played on the JS too. I played on practically all of those.
Another boat I've been wondering about, the Steamer Washington used to hit my hometown up in Missouri. Was that a St. Paul? That was St. Paul?
Yeah.
Washington, yeah.
Steamer Washington?
Sure.
I never did play on the Washington, but I remember we didn't get to talk about the Washington. That was that boat too.

I've been on that a lot of times in the Capitol. I might have heard your band when I was a kid up there going to high school in 19... Probably so? 1920 to 23, if you were on that early, I don't know. Or even later, I could hear, I went to college up in 1926. Those bands would go up there. Yeah. I never paid any attention. I was studying classical music then, so I didn't pay much attention to the jazz, but I'd stand there and listen to them and be fascinated too. It's quite possible I heard your band once and don't even remember or didn't know it at the time.
But the best trips of all, I think it was working on the Steamer Island Queen out of Cincinnati. Yeah, I liked that very much.
Did you stay there the whole summer?

Stayed there the whole summer. We were coming back to New Orleans and that's the time we had the ice all melting and the water all coming into Ohio River and the boat couldn't pass under the bridge. So I remember for two weeks we stayed right at the banks there and the captain said, well, we're going to wait until the water goes down. Which bridge was that?
Oh, I don't know.
I mean, is that the Steamer Island? Yeah, around there someplace we couldn't come down the river, you see.
Unless we went down to Cairo, Illinois.
Oh, no, no, no, not that far. And so we waited and we waited and you know what they did? You know the doom up there?
Oh, yeah.

They broke that thing down. Took it off temporarily so the boat could pass underneath the bridge. Took the bridge. I remember that. And we wasn't doing nothing for two weeks but we were drawing our salary right on.
Living on the boat.
That's right.
Well, I can't think of anything else to ask you now unless there's something else that you think of that you want to add about your life.
Well, no.
Have you really retired from music now?

Oh, I did. I did. I don't think I'll go back. I'm very well contented right there with my little business. You're happy here in California. Yeah, I'm happy right here in California. And I don't know just when I'll ever go back to New Orleans.
Oh, let's get that down on here too. When you came out here was 1950?
I came out here in 49. 49.
You opened this business here. In 1950.
You've been here all that time. That's right. Nine years.

That's right. I did. When I first came out here in 49 I opened up a little cafe on Avalon. Avalon. Avalon near Voynon. It was a very small place. Do you remember Dick Johnson's place over there? Never did. I don't remember his place. He gave it up about that time.
I think he left. Well, this fellow, Dink Johnson. Dink Johnson used to be a bass player. I don't remember. That's Bill. That's Bill Johnson.
Louse. Oh, well what did Dink Johnson, was he a poet on a train? Oh, he did.
Dink Johnson.
He played drums with Keppert and the Bach K for a while when they came out here. Oh, he did.
And sometimes he'd work a little bit as a pianist too. And he even played clarinet once with Ory.
He learned to play clarinet in eight years ago. Dink Johnson, I never did know that guy. Yeah. He was a bass player. Yeah, he was a bass player.
Yeah, he was a bass player. Yeah, he was a bass player. Yeah, he was a bass player.
Yeah, he was a bass player.

Yeah, he was a bass player. That's Bill. That's Bill. Bill Johnson, Louse. Oh, well what did Dink Johnson, was he a poet on a train? No, he played drums some and also played a little bit of piano. He played clarinet once with Ory. He learned to play clarinet in eight years ago. Bill Johnson, I never did know that guy. I knew him. I made some records of him once. He was dead now. But he was a younger brother of Bill Johnson. That plays right to the ballpark over there. Called Dink's Flicks right there at the corner where the Wrigley Field is. Yeah. It's a delicatessen now.
Well, I think that's about all the questions that I've been asked about.

I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. I was a little bit of a piano. But I remember all those things, you know.

But I remember all those things, you know. all those things you know but I think it was the greatest part of my life playing music all that many years. Yes that's something you never did. Yeah of course we didn't make any money we didn't have a chance to make any money in those days you know. Well by the way I might ask one second about making records do you remember? I remember making one record one with Faith Marvel Band.

That's what I thought there was one old okay record. One record I remember making. One was called Piano. Piano, Flyz and um. Get the other side. I don't have the record anymore. Some people still have it around.

Well that's been so long the bands are just beginning to make records. We made this right down in New Orleans. Right in New Orleans. We went up to the studio. They just began to make the records. Silestam had a fresh record.
I think we're just about out of tape here. I left the drum out of the tree.

segments.title: Opening: name and age
segments.summary: Desvigne gives his full name and says he is 65.

segments.title: Desvigne taking up trombone, hiring Louis Armstrong in Kenner
segments.summary: Desvigne explains he took trombone lessons when he could not find a trombonist, and hired Louis Armstrong on cornet for a job in Kenner.

segments.title: Manetta hired for the St. Louis boat band, Bob Sharper and Ed Allen
segments.summary: Manetta recalls being sent for from St. Louis, insisting Desvigne be taken too, the leadership passing from Sharper to Eddie Allen, and arriving in St. Louis.

segments.title: Sleeping on the boat and the first Monday night in St. Louis
segments.summary: Russell asks whether the men slept on the boat; Manetta recounts arriving and playing a colored Monday-night job.

segments.title: George Foster's warning and the gold band in Memphis
segments.summary: Foster warns Manetta about taking Desvigne over Sharper; Desvigne had to switch to a gold trumpet for the band and they rehearsed in Memphis.

segments.title: Boat pay and band members Walter Thomas, Floyd Casey, Eugene Sedric
segments.summary: Manetta recalls collecting pay on the boat and fellow players Walter Thomas, Floyd Casey and Eugene Sedric, whose father was a ragtime pianist.

segments.title: Where the boat musicians lived in St. Louis
segments.summary: Russell asks if the men took rooms in St. Louis; Desvigne says nobody lived on the boat except when travelling upriver.

segments.title: The trombone job at the Blue Rhythm Club and trumpeter Arnold Metoyer
segments.summary: Desvigne and Manetta recall a dance where the crowd wanted him on trumpet not trombone, and praise trumpeter Arnold Metoyer, who later led the Desvigne Orchestra.

segments.title: Head arrangements and playing the blues in Bogalusa
segments.summary: Desvigne says the band knew its arrangements by memory and tells of a Bogalusa crowd that only danced when they played the blues.

segments.title: Muscatine, Iowa dance and learning square-dance music
segments.summary: At a big dance in Muscatine the crowd preferred the other band's quadrille music, so Desvigne bought a book of that music and rehearsed it.

segments.title: Favorite trombonists
segments.summary: Asked for favorite trombonists, Desvigne names Vic Gaspard, Buddy Johnson, Benirap and Louis Nelson, who played well when sober.

segments.title: Roy Palmer giving trombone lessons and selling him a horn
segments.summary: Desvigne took trombone lessons from Roy Palmer, who sold him an old horn for a dollar and a half.

segments.title: Zue Robertson and the 101 Ranch offer; Bebe Ridley
segments.summary: Zue Robertson wanted to take him to the 101 Ranch show but his mother refused; then talk of Bebe Ridley.

segments.title: Kid Ory and advertising on the corner against rival bands
segments.summary: Desvigne worked alongside Kid Ory without being in his band, with competing bands advertising on the corner.

segments.title: Early bands heard as a boy: Olympia and Keppard
segments.summary: Desvigne names Freddie Keppard's Olympia band and its clarinetist and violinist, recalling he was too young to know them.

segments.title: Teaching, bus travel, and big band versus small band
segments.summary: He disliked teaching, travelled by bus through the Gulf states, and compares playing in big and small bands.

segments.title: First uniformed big band in New Orleans
segments.summary: Desvigne believes his was the first big band in New Orleans to wear uniforms, which others then copied.

segments.title: Identifying the members of the 1930s band photograph
segments.summary: Looking at a photograph of his big band, Desvigne names the pianist, saxophonists, drummer, trombonist Moran and others, and Louis Nelson's drinking.

segments.title: Riverboats played and Russell's memories of boat bands
segments.summary: They list the boats Desvigne played, including the Sydney, St. Paul and Capitol, and Russell recalls hearing boat bands as a youth.

segments.title: Summer on the Island Queen and the bridge delay on the Ohio
segments.summary: Desvigne's best trip was a summer on the Island Queen out of Cincinnati, stuck two weeks by high water at a bridge but still paid.

segments.title: Retirement in California and his cafe
segments.summary: He says he has retired from music, moved to California in 1949, and opened a small cafe on Avalon.

segments.title: Dink Johnson and the Johnson brothers
segments.summary: Talk turns to Dink Johnson, a drummer, bass player and pianist who played with Keppard and Ory.

segments.title: Closing reflections and an early New Orleans record
segments.summary: Desvigne calls music the greatest part of his life, mentions little money, and recalls an early record made in New Orleans before the tape ends.
